A$AP and Jaden address the death of Eric Garner. On July 17, 2014, Staten Island local Eric Garner was killed after being put in a fatal chokehold by a New York City police officer. As Garner lay on the ground, his last words, “I can’t breathe” became a symbol of police brutality and a rallying cry for the Black Lives Matter movement, appearing on t-shirts and even being made into a tribute song released by the Garner family.

In December of that same year, a Staten Island grand jury acquitted the police officer who put Garner in the choke hold, leading many protestors and civil rights activists to cry foul.

https://twitter.com/chancetherapper/status/731323875355545600

Prior to the release of Coloring Book, social media posts built hype for potential collaborations. On his Instagram, Ty Dolla posted a photo of him in the studio with Chance. Two weeks before the release of Chance’s third mixtape, he tweeted at Anderson .Paak, causing fans to speculate about a potential collaboration:

https://twitter.com/chancetherapper/status/710929805751881728?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw

This is the first collaboration between Ty Dolla $ign and Chance The Rapper, as well as the first collaboration between Chance and Anderson .Paak.

BJ The Chicago Kid and Donnie Trumpet, however, are frequent collaborators with Chance. BJ lent his vocals twice for Chance’s second mixtape, Acid Rap, specifically for “Good Ass Intro” and “Everybody’s Something.” Donnie is part of the group Social Experiment, which Chance is also a part of. Together they made Surf.

Interestingly, three of the singers who provide background vocals—BJ, Anderson and Ty Dolla—have all collaborated on one song before. They each provided vocals of “Church (West Coast Remix),” which is a remix of the original “Church,” a BJ The Chicago song featuring none other than Chance himself.

line: I’m pre-currency, post-language, anti-label

meaning:
Chance’s mindset is that music should be free, which is reflected in the fact that he has only released free music. In order to retain this freedom, he has avoided signing to a record label.

“Post-language” is a term implying that the poetry in question follows a significant period of literary activity, perhaps even defining its own period. Coloring Book is “post-language” as it marks a shift in Chance’s mindset and style; taking what was so successful about Acid Rap and blending it with recent inspirations. His artistry has matured and this maturation is exemplified throughout the entirety of the tape.

Chance’s string of “pre/post/anti/pro” may also be based off of late comedian George Carlin’s “Modern Man” where he uses a similar string in his opening monologue.

Exodus 34:1 has a likely influence on this line:

The Lord said to Moses, ‘Cut two tablets of stone like the former ones, and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the former tablets, which you broke.

The cracked screens from electronics Chance walked into Apple with are a reference to the “tablets” Moses cracked when he saw the Children of Israel worshiping a Golden Calf rather than their one true God. The second half of these tablets  was later cut by Moses, and God rewrote the prophetic inscription known as the ten commandments.

Chance has been fighting to keep his music free while also not signing with a label, instead shattering the monolithic hold Apple and others have over music. He mentions in “Angels” that he has “Steve giving out Apples for free,” rebelling against the traditional pay-for-song aspect of iTunes.

As Chance said in “Blessings”:

I don’t make songs for free, I make ‘em for freedom
Don’t believe in kings, believe in the Kingdom

Through the free release of Surf and Coloring Book, Chance has ensured free music for his fans and secured his own freedom to create music as he sees fit.

line: I speak of promised lands Soil as soft as mama’s hands Running water standing still Endless fields of daffodils and chamomile Rice under black beans
vault_lines: Running water standing still

Rice under black beans
meaning:
Chance begins by drawing inspiration from his Christian faith to speak of a utopian place of peace and happiness, reminiscent of the land of Milk and Honey referred to in the Book of Exodus. Chance also alluded to this in “Pusha Man”.

I’ll take you to land, where the lake made of sand
And the milk don’t pour and the honey don’t dance
And the money ain’t yours

He envisions the soil of this utopian land being as soft as his mothers hand; a hand that nurtured and raised him, helping him grow into the man he is today. He suggests that soil in the promised land will similarly nurture and foster spiritual growth.

Similarly, still water is generally not considered as safe as running water in nature, since the flow of running water acts as a natural filtration system. Chance suggests that the promised land is a place where even still water is turned to safe drinking water. Thematically this also can be compared to one of Jesus' most famous feats of turning water to wine.

Daffodils and chamomile are plants that are generally associated with happiness and peace through their visual appeal or calming properties when consumed in tea. Rice and beans are staple foods in practically all cultures, representative of the nourishment provided by this promised land.

The phrase “standing still” may also be a reference to the biblical verses Psalms 46:9-10.

He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire. Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.

As noted by Vice, ego death doesn’t necessarily have to be a psychedelic-induced experience, with Buddhists calling it “enlightenment” that can be achieved through meditation, and Sufi Muslims calling it ‘fana’. Regardless of how it is achieved or viewed, it’s often seen to be an awakening and profoundly introspective experience, with some noting a feeling of connection with the universe.

Ty uses the metaphor of ‘ego death’ to describe the effects that a failed relationship had on him and his personality. Or say, "Baby, let's put this back on the tree" 'cause
meaning:
Kanye West poses a twist to the Judeo-Christian narrative of Adam and Eve, found in Genesis 2 and Genesis 3. According to this well known creation story, God told the first human couple not to eat from the “tree of knowledge of good and evil” or else face certain death. The tree’s fruit is typically represented by an apple.



The ending of the second verse transitions into the refrain, with Kanye questioning the outcome of two extremes: condensing the forbidden fruit into a beverage and partaking willingly (modernizing the metaphor and highlighting how temptations can be repackaged in new, less obvious ways), or otherwise renouncing the physical embodiment of sin.

The latter connotes repentance and gratitude for all that God has provided: instead of yielding to temptation, opt for self-restraint, making a conscious decision to “put it back on the tree” (a call for personal growth and responsibility).

He also lamented the increasing prevalence of mass murder events on his January 2020 song “Darkness.”

Nevertheless, two of his songs have prompted backlash for displaying a seemingly cavalier attitude about the tragic event. The first was a December 2018 freestyle titled “Kick Off,” in which Em rapped:

Following the second wave of backlash, Mathers released a statement over Twitter in which he refused to back down, writing:

meaning:
Quavo is likely referring to actress Sharon Stone and more specifically, the femme fatale-esque characters she’s portrayed throughout her career. A femme fatale is an archetype of characters who are traditionally seductive, beautiful women whose alluring nature preludes eventful disaster for anyone who encounters them. Given how femme fatales tend to use their sexuality to manipulate others, it’s no wonder Quavo would describe Stone as “freaky,” or sexually adventurous given the nature of some of her more explicit roles.

In 1993, Stone portayed Carly Norris in Sliver, an erotic thriller where her character has an affair with a high-tech voyeur and unravels a mystery about her apartment’s previous tenant. A year prior, she appeared in perhaps her most iconic role, playing Catherine Tramell in Paul Verhoeven’s adaptation of Basic Instinct. In the film, Tramell is a crime novelist and main suspect in the murder of a rock star. She seduces the main detective on the case and the pair begin a dangerous game of cat and mouse.



Stone in Basic Instinct


Basic Instinct was Stone’s breakout role, and due in part to the erotic nature of the film, she was widely regarded as a sex symbol in the 1990s. In 2021, she wrote to Vanity Fair to discuss how this era of her career was a double-edged sword:


Many people ask me what it was like in my days of being a superstar. It was like this. Play ball or get off the field, girl.

My work reflects the times when I did have the opportunity to collaborate with the good and great directors, and I sat at their feet, learning everything I could for the times ahead. For I was not the chosen one, not the golden gal, just the sex symbol who could sometimes get the key part if she also happened to be sexy.

That picture was the biggest marketing campaign that any unknown has ever launched. Jay Leno talked about that picture, so did Regis and Kelly. It was in Time, Newsweek, People. It made me famous overnight.



In 2002, Watkins appeared in season one of ABC/MTV’s reality television series Making the Band 2. in 2003, Bentley was featured on Da Band’s Too Hot for T.V. in Cheers to Me, Mr. Bentley and Outkast’s 2003 album Speakerboxxx / The Love Below, in Good Day, Good Sir (Interlude). Later that year, Watkins served as a celebrity cameo in Outkast’s The Way You Move’s music video, then Kanye West’s The New Workout Plan in 2004.

Not only is Watkins known for being Diddy’s former personal assistant, The Boombox considers “Mr. Bentley” the world’s most famous umbrella holder.

meaning:
Howard references the 1965 Civil Rights marches from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama to promote voting rights for all in the United States of America. The violence instigated by Alabama State Troopers during the marches brought the movement to the forefront of the attention of the American public, as was instrumental in the passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

In 2014, the events of the marches were made into a film simply titled Selma which would go on to be nominated for an Oscar for “Best Motion Picture of the Year” and would win the Oscar for “Best Achievement in Music Written for Motion Pictures, Original Song” with the song “Glory.”  This is a clever play on the previous line and a reference to Oscar Grant.

At the time of the release of this song, protests were frequent in reaction to the slayings of unarmed black men throughout the country. Howard proclaims that “the new Selma is happening right now,” suggesting that another revolution leading to change will likely stem from this new wave of protest.

line: They saw Rodney, you saw a king
vault_lines: They saw Rodney, you saw a king
meaning:
On March 3rd, 1991, Rodney King fled the police in a high speed pursuit after being flagged for speeding on a Los Angeles freeway. At the conclusion of the chase, the pursuing officers brutally beat King before finally apprehending him. Footage of the brutal beatings made their way to the public and the officers were eventually acquitted of all wrongdoing in a trial, largely leading to the 1992 Los Angeles riots.

During the trial, King became something of a martyr to the black community across the country, as people became increasingly frustrated with the mistreatment blacks faced from police. Thus, while the officers only saw a black man evading arrest, Howard notes that the black community and specifically his mother whom he continues to address instead saw King as literally a king.

vault_lines: But I've had no regrets
meaning:
Sample: “A Lifetime” by The Brothers of Soul (1968)

The intro of “Model (You Ain’t No Model)” features the track “A Lifetime” by the Detroit soul group The Brothers of Soul. Released in 1968, the original song is a classic piece of Northern Soul that expresses a sentiment of unwavering, lifelong devotion.

CyHi often utilizes soul samples to ground his tracks in a classic, “soulful” aesthetic—a technique frequently seen in his collaborations with Kanye West. By opening with these specific lyrics, CyHi establishes a theme of long-term commitment and emotional investment that he proceeds to deconstruct in the verses.



The intro establishes a baseline of total devotion. By sampling a song that claims ‘no regrets’ for a lifetime of love, CyHi sets up a juxtaposition: he once gave this woman ‘model’ treatment and unconditional patience. However, as the song progresses, he reveals that once he realized she was just a ‘regular girl’ and not the high-status icon she portrayed, the ‘no regrets’ era ended. The sample represents the pedestal he once put her on, which the rest of the track proceed to knock down.

line: Walking out the court, thumbs up, John Gotti
vault_lines: Walking out the court, thumbs up, John Gotti
meaning:
This line is actually not a reference to infamous mob boss John Gotti, who died in a federal prison in 2002 from throat cancer.

Rather, it refers to his son, John Angelo Gotti, or “Junior” Gotti.



In 2004, Junior Gotti was charged in an 11-count racketeering indictment that included an alleged plot to kidnap Curtis Sliwa, founder of the Guardian Angels, as well as securities fraud, extortion and loansharking.

Three juries eventually deadlocked on the charges, the last in 2006, and federal prosecutors decided not to pursue a fourth trial.
But during the trial, when the verdict was being read, and Gotti was being acquitted, he turned at one point to his lawyers and family and gave a confident “thumbs up"—presumably to signal that they had done good job, or that he was happy with the outcome of the trial.

Gotti was arrested again In August 2008 and indicted on racketeering and murder conspiracy charges brought in Florida. This was eventually declared a mistrial, and federal prosecutors have indicated that they will not seek another trial against Gotti, saying that they could not find any credible witnesses.

In low income neighborhoods such as the one Lupe came from in Chicago, there is often a lack of job availability. This results in the people of the neighborhood turning to illegal activities such as drug dealing to make a profit. Lupe knows his people need another alternative to escape this lifestyle. Consequently, he’s asking god to provide his people with more job opportunities.

For example–Gallup measured the public’s perception of Martin Luther King Jr. in the 1960s, using a “scalometer” that asked the public to rate him on a +5 to a -5 scale. The resulting data show that King’s image became more negative as the years went on.

In 1963,  Martin Luther King had a 41% positive and a 37% negative rating; in 1964, it was 43% positive and 39% negative; in 1965, his rating was 45% positive and 45% negative; and in 1966 – the last Gallup measure of King using this scalometer procedure – it was 32% positive and 63% negative.

In 1999, Gallup used a special research procedure to determine the most admired individuals of the 20th century. Based on the results of both open-ended and closed-ended questions, Gallup calculated a list of the 18 people Americans admired most.

The person receiving the most votes was Mother Teresa: 49% of Americans said she was “one of the people I admire most from the century.” King was second, with 34% of the “most admired” votes.

meaning:
Here, former presidential candidate West celebrates the virtue of brevity. By lamenting the length of communications sent to him over various mediums, likely from a romantic partner, Mr. West scathingly condemns their excessive verbiage. This is cleverly emphasized by the repetition of the word “long” and the punctuating percussive beat.

However, as Mr. West seeks to edify rather than merely criticize, he suggests an alternative method of communication. In line with the theme of brevity, Mr. West states that his romantic partner “[needs] to get to the point already”. Thus, not only may Mr. West economize the use of his own time, but he also elucidates how his partner can engage in more efficient communication strategies which more clearly demonstrate the essence of their messaging. In this mastermind stroke, Mr. West uncovers a solution which achieves winnings for both parties in a positive-sum game.
